pll1d37c1-d1e3501.summary: Transition from the discussion of how all things are in God to how God is in things, with a caution about human ability to speak of it.
claims: The question of how God is in things follows on that of how things are in God.

pll1d37c1-d1e3504.summary: States the thesis: God, unchanging in himself, is present, powerful, and essential in every nature, place, and time, without definition, circumscription, or mutability.
claims: God is in every nature, place, and time without being defined, circumscribed, or changed.

pll1d37c1-d1e3507.summary: Adds the special modes: God dwells in holy spirits and souls by grace, and in Christ most excellently (Col 2:9), by the grace of union, not adoption.
claims: God dwells in the saints by grace.
In Christ God dwells by the grace of union, not of adoption.

pll1d37c1-d1e3523.summary: Justifies appeal to authorities, since these matters exceed human understanding and some may charge them with falsity.
claims: Doctrines beyond human understanding need patristic authority.

pll1d37c1-d1e3528.summary: Gregory: God is common to all things by presence, power, substance, yet is present more familiarly by grace to those who contemplate his works.
claims: God is in all things commonly, and by grace more intimately in some.

pll1d37c1-d1e3546.summary: Augustine: God, incorporeal and immutable, is wholly present to all things and to each wholly, but is possessed in varying degrees according to capacity, dwelling as in a temple.
claims: God is wholly present in all things and each, yet received differently.
Indwelling varies by the capacity of the receiver.

pll1d37c1-d1e3568.summary: Hilary: God's living power is nowhere absent and is everywhere, not in bodily manner.
claims: God is everywhere non-bodily, not absent anywhere.

pll1d37c1-d1e3585.summary: Ambrose: creatures are limited by nature, so the Holy Spirit, who is everywhere, is not a creature; omnipresence is proper to divinity.
claims: Omnipresence proves the Holy Spirit is not a creature.

pll1d37c1-d1e3604.summary: Ambrose continues: the Lord fills all things (Jer 23:24); the Spirit who fills the world is thus divine.
claims: Filling all things is proper to the Lord, hence the Spirit is divine.

pll1d37c1-d1e3634.summary: Concludes that God is in all creation essentially, presently, and potentially.
claims: God is in all creation essentially, presentially, and potentially.

pl-l1d37c1.summary: Opens the discussion of the modes in which God is in things: essentially, presently, and potentially in all things without limitation or change, and by grace in the saints and supremely in Christ by union. Supported by Gregory, Augustine, Hilary, and Ambrose.
claims: God is in all things by presence, power, and essence without limitation or mutability.
God is present in the saints by grace and in Christ by the grace of union.
Universal divine presence is a mark of divinity (against creaturely status of the Spirit).
